questions.q: How does a T-SQL parameter like @CustomerId INT translate into PL/SQL?
options: It keeps the @ sigil exactly as written in T-SQL
As a bare name with no sigil, explicitly marked IN (or OUT/IN OUT), conventionally p_ prefixed
It becomes a package-level variable instead of a parameter
PL/SQL procedures cannot take parameters, so it must become a global variable
questions.explain: PL/SQL drops the @ sigil, requires an explicit IN/OUT/IN OUT direction, and p_ prefixing is a common naming convention.

questions.q: T-SQL allows DECLARE @var statements scattered through a procedure body. How does PL/SQL handle local variable declarations?
options: PL/SQL also allows DECLARE anywhere inside BEGIN...END
Every local variable must be declared up front in one DECLARE (or IS, for named procedures) section before BEGIN
Local variables must be declared inside the EXCEPTION section
PL/SQL has no way to declare local variables at all
questions.explain: This is the block structure from Lesson 35 — DECLARE/IS always comes before BEGIN, with every local variable declared there.

questions.q: What is the single biggest structural change needed when translating a T-SQL procedure that ends in a bare result-set-returning SELECT?
options: Wrapping the SELECT in a WHILE loop
Converting the SELECT into a DBMS_OUTPUT.PUT_LINE call
Adding a SYS_REFCURSOR OUT parameter and OPENing it FOR the query, since PL/SQL has no free bare-SELECT-to-caller behavior
No change is needed — PL/SQL procedures return result sets exactly like T-SQL
questions.explain: T-SQL's bare SELECT streams back to the caller for free; PL/SQL requires an explicit REF CURSOR OUT parameter (Lesson 38) to replicate that behavior.

questions.q: How does T-SQL's IF @OrderCount = 0 BEGIN ... END translate into PL/SQL?
options: IF v_order_count = 0 THEN ... END, with no closing IF keyword needed
WHILE v_order_count = 0 LOOP ... END LOOP
IF v_order_count = 0 BEGIN ... END, unchanged from T-SQL syntax
IF v_order_count = 0 THEN ... END IF; — PL/SQL always requires THEN and END IF regardless of statement count
questions.explain: PL/SQL's IF always needs THEN and always closes with the two-word END IF, unlike T-SQL's BEGIN...END which is only needed for multi-statement branches.

questions.q: Why does the translated PL/SQL procedure add an EXCEPTION section with WHEN OTHERS, even though the original T-SQL version had no TRY...CATCH?
options: A production-quality PL/SQL translation should add defensive error handling, since an unhandled PL/SQL exception behaves differently from an unhandled T-SQL error
The original T-SQL procedure's PRINT statement requires a matching EXCEPTION block
WHEN OTHERS is mandatory syntax with no functional purpose
PL/SQL procedures are required by the compiler to always include an EXCEPTION section
questions.explain: Adding EXCEPTION/WHEN OTHERS costs nothing and is good defensive practice, even when translating from a T-SQL procedure that had no explicit error handling.
